summary: Gives the details for using Triple-DES to encrypt packets carried over PPP links. It is a stronger variant of the earlier DES-based specification. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is a way to lock the data on a direct computer-to-computer link. The lock is run three times in a row to make it harder to pick.

questions: what is the ppp triple-des encryption protocol
how does triple des work in ppp
subtitle: How to encrypt PPP packets with Triple-DES in CBC mode, negotiated through the PPP Encryption Control Protocol.

tldr.problem: PPP links can carry private traffic, but the generic PPP Encryption Control Protocol does not say how any one cipher is applied to packets.
tldr.mechanism: 3DESE applies DES-EDE3-CBC to the Protocol and Information fields, with three independent 56-bit keys, an 8-byte initial nonce offered during ECP negotiation, a 16-bit sequence number on each packet and self-describing padding.
tldr.outcome: It provides confidentiality only: nothing in it protects integrity, authenticates the sender or prevents replay, and the shared keys must come from some outside method.

today: RFC 2420 is a Proposed Standard from September 1998, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text builds on the earlier DES specification, RFC 2419.

sections.title: Purpose and Context
sections.content:
The goal of encrypting packets between two PPP implementations is to attempt to ensure the privacy of their communication. This document gives the specific details for using Triple-DES for that job, inside the framework of the generic PPP Encryption Control Protocol (ECP, RFC 1968) on top of PPP (RFC 1661).

The variant used is DES-EDE3-CBC. Because CBC mode chains blocks together, each packet carries a sequence number so the receiver can keep packets in order and detect lost ones.
sections.eli5: Two computers on one cable want to keep their chat private. This document says exactly how to scramble each message three times so only the other side can read it.

sections.title: The DES-EDE3-CBC Algorithm
sections.content:
An Initialization Vector (IV) is XORed with the first 64-bit (8 octet) plaintext block. The keyed DES function is then applied three times: an encryption (E), a decryption (D), then an encryption (E), each with an independent key (k1, k2 and k3). For later blocks, the previous ciphertext block is XORed with the current 8-octet plaintext block before the same three steps.

To decrypt, the order is reversed: decrypt with k3, encrypt with k2, decrypt with k1, then XOR with the previous ciphertext block. When all three keys are the same, DES-EDE3-CBC is equivalent to DES-CBC.
sections.eli5: Each block of the message is mixed with the scrambled block before it, then locked with key one, unlocked with key two and locked again with key three. Reading it back means doing the steps in reverse.

sections.title: Keys
sections.content:
The shared secret key is effectively 168 bits long. It is made of three independent 56-bit quantities used by DES. Each 56-bit subkey is stored as a 64-bit (8 octet) quantity, with the least significant bit of each octet used as a parity bit.

When keys are configured, those with incorrect parity or so-called weak keys SHOULD be rejected. The RFC does not say how the keys are exchanged; see the security section.
sections.eli5: There are three secret keys instead of one. The computers must agree on them beforehand, and bad keys that are too easy to guess should be refused.

sections.title: The 3DESE Option for ECP
sections.content:
An implementation offers 3DESE through an ECP Configuration Option. The option says the sender is offering to decrypt communications on the link this way, and can be read as a request for its peer to encrypt packets in this manner.

The option has a Type of 2, a Length of 10 and an Initial Nonce of 8 bytes. The peer uses the nonce to encrypt the first packet it sends after reaching the opened state. To guard against replay attacks, an implementation SHOULD offer a different value during each ECP negotiation.
sections.eli5: When the computers say hello, one of them hands over a random starting number. The other uses it to scramble its first message, and a fresh number should be used every time.

sections.title: The 3DESE Packet Format
sections.content:
An encrypted packet holds an Address field, a Control field, a zero octet, a one-octet Protocol ID, two sequence number octets and then the ciphertext. Address and Control MUST be present unless Address and Control Field Compression has been negotiated. Protocol Field Compression MAY be applied to the leading zero if negotiated.

The Protocol ID is 0x53 or 0x55. The latter indicates the Individual Link Encryption Control Protocol and that the ciphertext contains a Multilink fragment. The 16-bit sequence number is assigned by the encryptor, starting at 0 for the first packet sent once ECP has reached the opened state.
sections.eli5: Each scrambled message gets a small label on the front saying what kind of message it is and its number in the series, followed by the scrambled contents.

sections.title: Encrypting Packets
sections.content:
Once ECP is opened, the sender MUST NOT apply encryption to LCP packets or ECP packets. The encryption covers the Protocol and Information fields of a PPP packet, padded to a multiple of 8 bytes, and excludes the Address and Control fields. If the async control character map option has been negotiated, mapping is applied after the encryption has run.

For the first packet after ECP enters the opened state, the Initial Nonce is itself encrypted with 3DES before it is used.
sections.eli5: Everything about how the message is carried is left plain, but the message itself is scrambled. The setup chat that arranges the scrambling is never scrambled.

sections.title: Padding and Packet Loss
sections.content:
DES works on blocks of 8 octets, so shorter data must be padded. The RFC requires Self Describing Padding with a Maximum Pad Value of 8: the plaintext is padded with the octets 1, 2, 3 and so on. Plaintext already a multiple of 8 octets may need a further 8 octets (1 to 8), but these MUST only be appended if the last octet of the plaintext was 8 or less. After decryption, the receiver strips the padding and SHOULD discard the frame if the padding does not match the scheme.

Loss shows up as a gap in sequence numbers. If packet N - 1 is lost, packet N cannot be decrypted because it needs the last ciphertext block of N - 1, but packet N + 1 and later can be decrypted normally because they only need the last block of the previous packet.
sections.eli5: Messages are cut into 8-byte pieces, and the last piece is topped up with counting-number filler. If one message is lost, the very next one is spoiled too, but the ones after that are fine.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This proposal provides confidentiality only. It describes no mechanism for integrity, authentication or nonrepudiation, so it does not guarantee that a received message was not modified in transit through replay, cut-and-paste or active tampering. It also does not authenticate the source of a packet.

It relies on external, unspecified methods for retrieving shared secrets, and proposes no new technology for privacy. Any limits of the 3DES cipher, and the way the secrets are protected and retrieved, apply to this use.
sections.eli5: The lock keeps strangers from reading the message, but it does not prove who sent it or stop someone from changing it on the way.

fields.name: Address
fields.desc: Present unless ACFC has been negotiated.

fields.name: Control
fields.desc: Present unless ACFC has been negotiated.
Leading zero; may be compressed if Protocol Field Compression is negotiated.

fields.desc: High octet of the 16-bit sequence number.

fields.desc: Low octet of the 16-bit sequence number.
